# Scale a recipe up or down with an AI assistant

> **In short:** Paste any recipe into an AI assistant and ask for a different number of servings — it recalculates the ingredients for you in seconds. The one thing to know: baking recipes with leavening agents (like baking soda or yeast) don't always scale in a perfectly straight line, so it's worth double-checking those.

You've found the perfect cookie recipe — but it makes 36 cookies and you only want 12 for a small dinner. Or you've got a soup recipe for 4 and your in-laws are coming, so you need to stretch it to 8. The math itself is simple (multiply by 1.5, divide by 3), but it's easy to slip up, especially when you're dealing with fractions like ⅔ cup or 1.25 teaspoons.

An AI assistant can do that math for you in a few seconds, and — bonus — it can also flag when a recipe won't scale cleanly. Think of it like a calculator that happens to know a little about cooking.

This guide works with any AI assistant you already use: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Le Chat by Mistral, or DeepSeek. The steps look almost identical across all of them.

## Before you start
- An AI assistant you can type into (free or paid — most require a free account; any tier works for this task).
- The recipe you want to scale, with ingredient amounts and the original serving size clearly written.
- About 3–5 minutes total.

## Step 1 — Open your AI assistant and start a new chat
Open the AI assistant of your choice on your phone or computer. If you're using a mobile app, look for a **"New chat"** button or a **pencil/edit icon** at the top of the screen — tap it. If you're on a website, just find the empty chat box at the bottom of the page. The important part is starting fresh: don't paste the recipe into an old conversation about something else, because the assistant can get confused if it has too much unrelated context to think about. A blank chat gives you the cleanest, most focused answer.
💬 Example: a "New chat" button at the top of the ChatGPT app, or a sparkle icon ✨ next to an empty text box on Gemini.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty text box with a blinking cursor and no previous messages above it.

## Step 2 — Paste your recipe into the chat
Tap inside the text box and paste your full recipe, including the ingredient list and the cooking instructions. You can paste from a website, a notes app, or a photo of a cookbook page (look for a **paperclip or image icon** next to the text box — tap it, then choose your photo). Make sure the recipe actually includes the ingredient amounts and the number of servings it was originally written for, because the assistant needs both to scale it correctly. If your recipe just says "a handful of flour," the assistant can only guess. The more specific the numbers, the more accurate your scaled recipe will be.
💬 Example: paste a recipe that begins with "Serves 6. Ingredients: 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 3 eggs…"
You'll know it worked when the recipe text appears in the chat box, either as plain text or as a small image thumbnail.

## Step 3 — Tell the assistant your new serving size
Below your pasted recipe, type a short instruction telling the assistant what you want. Be specific: tell it the original number of servings and the new number you want, and ask it to recalculate the ingredients. If you're scaling up for a crowd (say, 4 to 12), mention that too — sometimes the assistant will suggest splitting the recipe across two pans or adjusting the cooking time, which is genuinely useful. If you don't ask about pans or time, the assistant may just give you the math without those helpful extras.
💬 Example: "This recipe serves 4. Please scale it down to serve 2 and keep all the ingredient amounts in the same units (cups, tablespoons, teaspoons). Also tell me if I need to adjust the cooking time."
You'll know it worked when the assistant replies with a new ingredient list that matches your requested serving size — usually in just a few seconds.

## Step 4 — Ask follow-up questions about tricky parts
Some recipes don't scale in a perfectly straight line. Baking recipes that rely on baking soda, baking powder, or yeast (think cakes, breads, muffins) often need a little less leavening per cup of flour when you scale up — otherwise the texture can turn out off. Spices and salt are similar: doubling a curry recipe doesn't always mean doubling the chili powder, or it becomes inedible. A good follow-up prompt asks the assistant to flag any of these issues specifically. This step is what turns a quick calculation into genuinely useful cooking advice, and it only takes an extra sentence.
💬 Example: "Does anything in this recipe not scale cleanly? Should I adjust the baking soda or salt differently when doubling?"
You'll know it worked when the assistant either confirms everything is fine, or points out one or two ingredients to be careful with and suggests specific adjustments.

## Step 5 — Save or copy the scaled recipe
Once the scaled recipe looks right, you have a few options. You can highlight the assistant's reply and copy it into a notes app, email it to yourself, or ask the assistant to format it as a printable shopping list. Some apps have a **copy** button at the bottom of the reply — look for two overlapping squares or a small clipboard icon. If you're cooking from your phone, ask the assistant to make a separate checklist of just the ingredients so you can tap them off as you shop. Always glance at the AI's reply before you start cooking — it saves the heartbreak of realizing halfway through that something doesn't look right.
💬 Example: "Can you turn just the ingredient list into a numbered shopping list I can check off in the store?"
You'll know it worked when the scaled recipe is saved somewhere you can find it later (notes app, email, or screenshot) and is easy to read while you cook.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting only the ingredient names without the amounts.** If your recipe says "flour, sugar, eggs" with no numbers, the assistant has nothing to multiply. Always paste the full recipe with quantities.
- **Forgetting to mention the original serving size.** Without knowing whether the recipe serves 2 or 10, the assistant can't calculate the right ratio. Tell it both numbers in your prompt.
- **Trusting scaled baking recipes without a sanity check.** Breads, cakes, and other recipes with leavening agents are sensitive to overscaling. Ask the assistant in Step 4 whether anything needs special handling, and use your own judgment when the numbers look unusual.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** You can cook for one, two, or twenty without hunting for a "perfectly sized" recipe online. Found a great dinner-party recipe that serves 12 but you're cooking for 4? Scale it down in seconds.
- **For entertaining or potlucks:** When you're asked to bring something "for 8 people" and your favorite recipe makes 24 cookies, you can adjust in seconds instead of doing mental math at the grocery store.
- **If you're new to AI assistants:** This is one of the most beginner-friendly tasks you can try. You don't need to learn prompt engineering or special techniques — just paste, ask, and review.

## Try it now
Open any AI assistant on your phone right now, paste the recipe of whatever you're planning to cook this week, and ask it to scale the recipe to the number of people you're feeding. Three minutes, start to finish.
